The Mathematical Contract: What reach.rate Computes, Exactly

Jonathan Payne, Environment Agency Flood Forecasting

November 2026

Source: vignettes/mathematical_contract.Rmd
mathematical_contract.Rmd

Audience: technical. You need to know exactly what is computed, to check a rating against it or to reimplement it.

This is the document to check a rating against. It states every equation the package fits and applies, the units, the rules for awkward values, how a fit is chosen, what “converged” means, and what each interval does and does not cover. Where the package does something a reader might not expect, this says so plainly, in a section called what the package does not do.

Each statement here is held by a test in tests/testthat/test-contract.R, which fails if the code and this document disagree.

The equation

A rating limb is

\[Q = C\,(H - a)^{n}, \qquad H > a,\]

and zero for \(H \le a\).

symbol meaning unit
\(Q\) discharge m\(^3\)/s
\(H\) stage m
\(a\) the stage at which flow ceases m
\(n\) the exponent none
\(C\) the coefficient m\(^{3-n}\)/s

\(C\) carries units that depend on \(n\), so a \(C\) is only comparable with another \(C\) when the exponents are close.

The offset is subtracted: \((H - a)\). Some systems write \((H + a)\), in which the same offset has the opposite sign. Using one system’s value in the other’s equation moves the curve by twice the offset and gives no error. convert_offset_convention() changes the sign of a and nothing else, because \(C(H + a')^n = C(H - a)^n\) exactly when \(a' = -a\). Converting there and back returns the original values. It does not change a stage datum.

external <- data.frame(lower_level = 0.5, upper_level = 3, C = 4.1, a = -0.35, n = 1.6)
internal <- convert_offset_convention(external)   # from "add" to "subtract"
internal$a
#> [1] 0.35
# Both tables describe one curve:
external$C * (1.8 + external$a)^external$n
#> [1] 7.429724
internal$C * (1.8 - internal$a)^internal$n
#> [1] 7.429724

Limbs

A rating is a set of limbs, each with its own \(C\), \(a\) and \(n\) and a stage range. rate_optimise() fits each limb independently to the gaugings that fall in its range. It does not impose continuity at a breakpoint, and detect_rc_gaps() and align_limb_equations() exist to find and close any gap. rate_optimise_segmented() fits one joint model in which continuity is automatic (see the section on the segmented model).

Which limb a gauging belongs to. When fitting, a gauging is assigned to the limb whose range contains it, with the range closed on the upper side: limb 1 is \([h_0, h_1]\) and later limbs are \((h_{j-1}, h_j]\). A gauging exactly on a breakpoint is fitted into the lower limb.

When applying a rating the rule is the other way round. A stage is assigned by the half-open ranges \([h_{j-1}, h_j)\), with the last limb closed, so a stage exactly on a breakpoint is applied with the upper limb. For a continuous rating the discharge is the same either way. For a rating with a gap at the breakpoint it is not, and the gap check is what reveals it.

Outside the range. A stage below the first limb or above the last is computed with the nearest limb and flagged extrapolated. The equation is continued, not bounded.

Applying a rating

For a stage \(H\) in limb \(j\),

\[Q = \begin{cases} C_j\,(H - a_j)^{n_j} & H > a_j \\ 0 & H \le a_j \end{cases}\]

A stage of NA gives NA. The inverse, from discharge to stage, is

\[H = a_j + (Q / C_j)^{1/n_j},\]

for \(Q > 0\), with the limb chosen by comparing \(Q\) with the discharge at each limb’s bounds. A discharge of zero, a negative discharge or NA gives NA stage, because zero discharge corresponds to every stage at or below \(a\) and has no single answer. The inverse is only defined where discharge rises across the limbs; it refuses a rating where it does not.

How well a stage is supported

apply_rating() does not only compute a discharge. It says what the stage rests on, in a support column, by comparing it with five stage ranges (rating_support()): the range of the gaugings, the range of any modelled evidence, the range the equations are fitted over, the operational range if one has been stated, and the numerical range where the equations give a finite number.

support the stage is
interpolation_observed inside the range of the gaugings
interpolation_mixed inside the range of all the evidence, but outside the gaugings
model_supported inside the fitted range, with no evidence there
extrapolation beyond the fitted range
outside_operational_range beyond the stated operational limits (this outranks the rest)

Only gaugings count as observation. A modelled value, a cross-section or structure computation, and a point read off another rating are evidence that shapes a rating, and are kept apart from measurements. A stage beyond the numerical range is an error, since the discharge would not be a number. Support is a statement about the evidence, not the fit statistics: a limb that fits its gaugings very closely is still an extrapolation above the highest of them.

The two objectives

Each limb is fitted by minimising a weighted sum of squares over its \(m\) gaugings \((H_i, Q_i)\) with weights \(w_i\) (all 1 unless age weighting is on).

Absolute (objective = "absolute", the default of rate_optimise() and of the other fitters today):

\[\min_{C,a,n}\ \sum_{i=1}^{m} w_i\,\big(Q_i - C\,(H_i - a)^{n}\big)^2 .\]

Relative (objective = "relative"; the planned guided workflow will make this its default):

\[\min_{C,a,n}\ \sum_{i=1}^{m} w_i\,\big(\ln Q_i - \ln C - n\,\ln(H_i - a)\big)^2 .\]

The relative objective is a fit in log space. It needs every \(Q_i > 0\) and every \(H_i > a\). For small relative errors it is close to minimising \(\sum w_i\,\big((Q_i - \hat Q_i)/\hat Q_i\big)^2\), which is why it suits gaugings whose error scales with the reading.

The two give the same answer when the data lie exactly on a curve and different answers otherwise. Neither is “right”. The choice is a statement about how gauging error behaves, and the objectives vignette (vignette("objective_guide")) works through when they diverge.

Diagnostics are always on the discharge scale, whichever objective was used: rmse_cms, r_squared, rmse_pct and the error columns are recomputed from the fitted coefficients as \(Q_i - C(H_i - a)^n\), so the two objectives’ results can be compared directly. rmse_cms is the unweighted root mean square, \(\sqrt{\tfrac1m \sum (Q_i - \hat Q_i)^2}\).

Here is the absolute objective for three gaugings, worked by hand and then by the package’s own equation.

H <- c(1.5, 2.5, 3.5)
Q <- c(2.1, 5.5, 10.6)
C <- 2; a <- 0.5; n <- 1.5
modelled <- C * (H - a)^n
modelled
#> [1]  2.000000  5.656854 10.392305
residual <- Q - modelled
round(residual, 4)
#> [1]  0.1000 -0.1569  0.2077
sum(residual^2)                       # the absolute objective, weights 1
#> [1] 0.07774053
sum((log(Q) - log(C) - n * log(H - a))^2)   # the relative objective
#> [1] 0.003562787

Weighting by age

Age weighting is opt-in. With age_halflife set, a gauging of age \(t\) days has weight

\[w = w_{\min} + (1 - w_{\min})\;0.5^{\,t / t_{1/2}},\]

where \(t_{1/2}\) is age_halflife, \(w_{\min}\) is age_min_weight (default 0.1) and age is measured back from reference_datetime (default: the most recent gauging in the data). Age is clamped at zero, so a gauging dated after the reference has weight 1, not more. Weights are not normalised.

The floor exists so that an old gauging is never weighted to nothing. It is not magnitude-aware: an old extreme flood and an old ordinary gauging decay identically.

age_days <- c(0, 365, 730, 3650)
0.1 + 0.9 * 0.5^(age_days / 365)      # half-life one year, floor 0.1
#> [1] 1.0000000 0.5500000 0.3250000 0.1008789

Without age_halflife every weight is 1 and a supplied gauging_datetime changes nothing about the fit.

Zero and negative values

input absolute objective relative objective
negative discharge refused refused
zero discharge accepted refused (log of zero)
NA, NaN, infinite stage or discharge refused refused
negative stage accepted (stage is relative to a datum) accepted
stage with no spread refused refused

A limb needs at least 3 gaugings, because it has three parameters. The check that returns advice and not an error, validate_gaugings(), warns about zero discharge and treats a negative discharge as a technical failure.

Bounds on the parameters

For each limb the three parameters are box-constrained:

\[C \ge 10^{-6}, \qquad a \le h_{\min} - 10^{-6}, \qquad n \ge 10^{-6},\]

where \(h_{\min}\) is the lowest stage among that limb’s gaugings. The bound on \(a\) keeps every gauging above the zero-flow stage, so \((H_i - a) > 0\) for all of them. n_bounds = c(lower, upper) replaces the bounds on \(n\), and lower == upper fixes it. A limb is flagged near_bound when \(n\) is within 0.01 of either bound, or \(a\) is within 1% of the limb’s stage width of its upper bound.

A fit that sits on a bound is a fit the data did not decide. The flag exists so that this is visible.

Starting values and the multi-start rule

With multi_start = TRUE (the default) each limb is fitted from six starting points, then the best valid result is kept. With \(a_0 = 0\) unless the upper bound of \(a\) is negative, in which case $a_0 = $ that bound \(- 0.01\), the starts are:

  1. \(C = 1,\ a = a_0,\ n = 1\)
  2. \(C = 1,\ a = a_0,\ n = 1.5\)
  3. \(C = 1,\ a = a_0,\ n = 2\)
  4. \(C = \operatorname{median}(Q)/(\operatorname{median}(H) - a_0)^{1.5},\ a = a_0,\ n = 1.5\)
  5. \(C = 1,\ a = a_0 - 0.25\,(h_{\max} - h_{\min}),\ n = 1\)
  6. a log-log estimate: regress \(\ln Q\) on \(\ln(H - h_{\min} + 0.1)\) for the exponent and coefficient, with \(a = h_{\min} - 0.1\), the coefficient floored at 0.01 and the exponent at 0.1. This is omitted if the regression fails.

Each start is clipped into the bounds. An attempt is valid if the fitted equation is finite and does not decrease across a grid of 20 stages spanning the limb (30 across the range for the segmented model); a decrease of more than \(10^{-9}\) fails. Among the valid attempts the one with the smallest weighted sum of squares on the objective’s own scale is kept, whether or not the optimiser reported convergence (see the next section): the weighted absolute sum for the absolute objective, the weighted log-scale sum for the relative one. If no attempt is valid the fit stops with an error. Every attempt, selected or not, is recorded in @fit_starts.

This ranks attempts on the quantity each one minimised. Earlier versions ranked them on the unweighted sum of squares even when age weights were used, which chose between local optima by a criterion nobody had optimised. The two agree when there are no weights.

Convergence and identifiability

Each fit is a Levenberg-Marquardt least-squares fit (minpack.lm::nlsLM) with at most 100 iterations (300 for the segmented model) and the optimiser’s default tolerances. It stops when the relative change in the sum of squares, or in the parameters, falls below \(\sqrt{\epsilon} \approx 1.5 \times 10^{-8}\), with \(\epsilon\) the machine epsilon. The optimiser’s default limit of 400 function calls would stop a fit at about 94 iterations, before the iteration limit, so the call limit is raised to twenty times the iteration limit and the documented limit is the one in force.

Every limb of a fit records what happened, in stable columns of @limbs (and of @coefficients for the segmented model). Where the optimiser does not supply a value the column is NA, meaning not assessed, never a guess.

column meaning
converged the optimiser reports convergence (stop codes 1 to 4)
convergence_code, convergence_message its own stop code and message; -1 is the iteration limit
iterations iterations used by the fit that was kept
objective_value the weighted objective of Section “The two objectives”, at the kept fit
bound_hits parameters on a bound: C_lower, a_upper, n_lower, n_upper, comma separated; "" for none
multi_start_spread how far near-optimal starts disagree in discharge (see below)
parameter_correlation the largest absolute correlation between two parameter estimates
condition_number the condition number of the Jacobian with columns scaled to unit length

In @fit_starts, an attempt has converged (the optimiser’s own report) and valid (the domain and monotonicity check above) as separate columns, together with its stop code, message and iteration count.

Converged does not mean good, and unconverged does not mean bad. Among the valid attempts the package keeps the one with the lowest objective, whether or not it converged. A flat valley in the objective lets the optimiser creep for the whole iteration limit while the fit is already practically optimal, and a converged attempt can sit on a bound with a much worse objective. Ranking on convergence would sometimes choose the worse fit. So the choice is made on the objective, and the report says whether the kept attempt converged. When it did not, rate_optimise() and rate_optimise_segmented() warn, and say how the optimiser stopped.

multi_start_spread makes the difference visible. It is the largest difference in fitted discharge, across the limb, between the chosen solution and any other valid attempt whose objective is within 5% of it, as a fraction of the limb’s peak discharge. It is 0 when no other attempt is that close and NA when fewer than two attempts were valid or only one start was used. A large value means two almost equally good fits predict different discharges: the data do not choose between them. A small value alongside wandering parameters means the opposite: the curve is well determined though its coefficients are not.

parameter_correlation near 1, or a condition_number in the thousands, says two parameters trade off against each other. Neither is a verdict; they say where to look first.

Checks on the equations, and when a rating is refused

After a fit, rating_invariants() checks the rating’s own equations, without reference to its gaugings, and returns a FlodeAssessment. It answers whether the equations are mathematically usable. It does not say whether the rating is a good one.

A technical check can fail:

  • every \(C\), \(a\) and \(n\) is finite, and \(C\) and \(n\) are positive;
  • limb stage ranges are finite, ascending and contiguous;
  • discharge is finite and not negative at 25 stages in each limb;
  • discharge does not decrease as stage rises within a limb;
  • the discharge at the top of each limb is no lower than at the top of the limb before, so each discharge belongs to one limb;
  • discharge to stage and back reproduces the discharge to within \(10^{-6}\) (relative);
  • where bootstrap draws exist, each parameter’s lower, median and upper bounds are in order;
  • for a fit made directly by the optimiser, each parameter is inside the bounds it was given.

A hydrometric check can only warn: no gap or overlap between adjacent limbs’ stage ranges, discharge continuous across each junction (within 1% by default), and each limb’s zero-flow stage at or below its lower stage. That last one is a warning because discharge is zero at and below \(a\), so a limb that starts below it is a legitimate way to write a table, but part of the limb then carries no flow.

A failure stops the operation it makes meaningless. apply_rating() refuses a rating that fails any technical check except the two that concern the inverse, and says which check failed. apply_rating_inverse() refuses any failure. A drop in discharge at the top of a limb, for example, leaves stage to discharge well defined, so forward application proceeds, but makes the inverse ambiguous, so the inverse is refused. A warning never blocks.

The checks are evaluated when asked for, not stored on the object, so they always describe the rating as it now stands, including after a change to it. The same two facts are on the printed rating, as separate lines, because a fit can converge to an invalid equation and a valid equation can come from a fit that did not converge:

set.seed(7)
h <- seq(0.4, 3, by = 0.05)
q <- 3.2 * h^1.6 * exp(rnorm(length(h), sd = 0.03))
print(rate_optimise(q, h, control = 1.5))
#> <FlodeRating> 2 limb(s), origin: independently_fitted, lifecycle: draft
#>   converged: yes (2 of 2 limbs)
#>   valid: yes, with 1 warning (limb_continuity)
#> 
#>     limb lower_stage_m upper_stage_m        C           a        n   rmse_cms
#>    <int>         <num>         <num>    <num>       <num>    <num>      <num>
#> 1:     1           0.4           1.5 3.452241  0.03394668 1.552369 0.09401666
#> 2:     2           1.5           3.0 1.942301 -0.35539746 1.872624 0.26140031
#>    r_squared
#>        <num>
#> 1: 0.9968900
#> 2: 0.9949382

What the intervals mean

Asymptotic standard errors (C_se_asymp, a_se_asymp, n_se_asymp) are the square roots of the diagonal of the fit’s estimated covariance matrix under the usual linearised least-squares theory. They are always computed, and are NA when that matrix is singular. They assume the model is correct, errors are independent with constant variance on the fitted scale, and the sample is large enough for the linear approximation to hold. A limb with few gaugings, or whose parameters sit on a bound, does not meet that.

Bootstrap draws (n_boot > 0). Within each limb, gaugings are resampled with replacement, and the limb is refitted to the resample with the same objective, weights and bounds, starting from the original fitted values. A resample with fewer than 3 distinct stages or no stage spread is rejected. A refit that errors is recorded as a failed draw with its reason. Standard errors are the standard deviation of the successful draws, and the 2.5%, 50% and 97.5% points are their percentiles. A warning is issued when the successful fraction falls below min_boot_success (default 0.8).

Limb boundaries are held fixed across draws. A draw is not checked for the validity conditions that select the main fit, and because each starts from the fitted values, draws tend to stay near the selected solution and may understate how far another solution is.

apply_rating_interval() applies every successful bootstrap draw to a stage, using that draw’s coefficients and the original limb boundaries, and reports for each stage the mean, the median, a geometric standard error and the lower and upper percentiles at conf_level.

set.seed(3)
stage_m <- seq(0.5, 3, length.out = 25)
discharge_cms <- 3 * (stage_m - 0.2)^1.6 * exp(rnorm(25, sd = 0.04))
fit <- rate_optimise(discharge_cms, stage_m, n_boot = 100, boot_seed = 1)
draws <- rating_bootstrap(fit)
at <- data.frame(stage = 2)
by_package <- apply_rating_interval(at, draws)
by_hand <- draws$C * (2 - draws$a)^draws$n
c(package = by_package$discharge_lower, by_hand = quantile(by_hand, 0.025, names = FALSE))
#>  package  by_hand 
#> 7.520575 7.520575

What this interval covers is uncertainty in the fitted coefficients that comes from the finite set of gaugings. It does not cover:

  • error in the stage measurement, or in the gaugings’ own discharge beyond what shows up as scatter;
  • a shift in the rating over time;
  • the choice of equation form, or of where the breakpoints are;
  • the spread of a new gauging around the curve. It is an interval for the rating’s discharge at that stage, not a prediction interval for the next gauging.

Treat it as the width the data support, which is a lower bound on the width a user should plan for.

The segmented model

rate_optimise_segmented() fits one joint equation over the whole range, adapted from Hodson et al. (2024):

\[Q = C\,\max(H - b_1,\,0)^{n_1}\ \prod_{j \ge 2} \big(\max(H - b_j,\,0) + 1\big)^{n_j}.\]

\(b_1\) is the stage of zero flow. Each later factor is exactly 1 at and below its own breakpoint \(b_j\), so continuity is automatic. Above \(b_j\) the local exponent of the curve changes. It is fitted by the same least squares and objectives as above, not by the full Bayesian inference of the original paper, so there are no priors and no posterior. The interior breakpoints are held at control unless estimate_breakpoints = TRUE, in which case the loss surface is not convex and results can depend on the start. Multi-start selection and the weighting are as for rate_optimise().

What the package does not do

These are the places where the package is narrower than a reader might assume. They are collected here so none is found by surprise.

  • Limbs from rate_optimise() are not forced to meet. A gap or overlap at a breakpoint is reported by the gap tools, not prevented.
  • A gauging on a breakpoint is fitted with the lower limb and applied with the upper one.
  • A fit that did not converge is still returned, with a warning and converged = FALSE, when it has the lowest objective. It is not an error.
  • Bootstrap draws start from the fitted solution and are not validity checked.
  • No interval includes stage error, rating shift or equation-form error.
  • The offset convention is the only one handled. A stage datum shift is not.
  • Breakpoints are supplied or suggested, not estimated, except in the segmented model with estimate_breakpoints = TRUE.

Checking this against the package

The equations printed in a fit’s provenance are the ones in this document.

absolute <- rate_optimise(discharge_cms, stage_m)
relative <- rate_optimise(discharge_cms, stage_m, objective = "relative")
rating_provenance(absolute)$fitting_equation
#> [1] "Q = C(H - a)^n"
rating_provenance(relative)$fitting_equation
#> [1] "log(Q) = log(C) + n*log(H - a)"

And the fitted coefficients minimise the objective written above. At a minimum the objective cannot be reduced by moving any coefficient, so every small step away gives a larger value.

limb <- rating_limbs(absolute)
objective <- function(par) sum((discharge_cms - par[1] * (stage_m - par[2])^par[3])^2)
here <- c(limb$C, limb$a, limb$n)
steps <- c(1e-3, 1e-3, 1e-3)
worse <- vapply(1:3, function(k) {
  up <- here; up[k] <- up[k] + steps[k]
  down <- here; down[k] <- down[k] - steps[k]
  min(objective(up), objective(down)) > objective(here)
}, logical(1))
worse
#> [1] TRUE TRUE TRUE
